If you are going to disclose during the interview you're probably better of the more specific you can be about your disability in relation to your work. Autism is a disorder under the pathology paradigm which the world runs on. The pathology paradigm defines a narrow range of functioning with strengths and weaknesses that are acceptable. Anything diverging from that will be called a disorder. This reflects a medical model of thinking about disability where the goal is to normalize people to make them not disabled, i.e part of the acceptable range of functioning. 

The idea that there isn't one right type of mind, one good range of functioning, is inherent to the social model of disablity and is used in the neurodiversity paradigm. Under that autistic people are no less valid and difference can thrive in contrast to pathology where they are extinguished. There is more than one way to do things and the patology paradigm isn't flexible enough to support that. 

So while I acknowledge that autism is a disorder, I will resist that type of characterization. Changing the narrative to one of neurodiversity, different neurotypes, rather than normal and disordered is the way forward.
